To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
bioremediation of oil on shoreline environments is an effective oil spill response technique.

(1) bioremediation of oil spilled on shorelines can be an effective countermeasure, (2) the efficacy of bioremediation depends on a number of factors, including the environmental setting, the type and amount of bioremediant, and the bioremediant application technique, and (3) bioremediants are not toxic to shoreline biota.
bioremediation is an effective countermeasure to oil spills on shorelines and that bioremediations agents and procedures are available for use on cobble, sand beaches, salt marshes, and mudflats.

the development of effective bioremediation procedures that will be useful to coastal resource managers and spill response personnel.
the development of effective, safe, and environmentally sound bioremediation techniques for use on shoreline environments.
the development of effective and safe bioremediation techniques and the development of guidelines to assist in their use.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
bioremediation is a very effective countermeasure for oil spilled on shoreline ecosystems, provided that it is applied in the right way, at the right place and at the right time.
bioremediation of oil on shorelines is a proven technology.

bioremediation is effective in accelerating oil biodegradation rates and that the efficacy is dependent on the type of shoreline environment, the type of oil, and the type and concentration of the bioremediation agent used.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
bioremediation can be an effective oil countermeasure for use on shoreline environments.
the development of bioremediation procedures and the evaluation of bioremediants has been successful and the procedures are now routinely used to treat oil on shoreline environments.

the bioremediation of oil spills on shoreline environments is a viable and effective oil spill counter measure, but the use of bioremediation in response to an oil spill should only be considered after all other options have been exhausted.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in the right conditions, bioremediating agents can accelerate the natural biotransformation of oil in the field, but their effectiveness is highly dependent upon the environmental conditions, the type of oil, the type of shoreline environment, the bioremediating agent(s) and the timing of application.
the use of a bioremediation agent is not always necessary.

the most effective bioremediation techniques are those which are site specific and are designed to maximize natural biodegradation processes by enhancing the availability of oil to indigenous microorganisms and by providing a source of nitrogen and phosphorus.
